source.title: Scaling Monosemanticity: Extracting Interpretable Features from Claude 3 Sonnet
source.authors: Adly Templeton; Tom Conerly; Jonathan Marcus; Jack Lindsey; Trenton Bricken; Brian K. Chen; Adam Pearce; Craig Citro; E. Ameisen; Andy Jones; Hoagy Cunningham; N. Turner; Callum McDougall; M. MacDiarmid; Alex Tamkin; Esin Durmus; Tristan Hume; Francesco Mosconi; C. D. Freeman; T. Sumers; E. Rees; Joshua Batson; Adam S. Jermyn; Shan Carter; Chris Olah; T. Henighan

record.tranche_reason: The study reports that the extracted feature set is incomplete and that features split as dictionary size increases, qualifying claims that SAE features are complete, stable, canonical units. It also extends SAE feature extraction to Claude 3 Sonnet, but T5 is closer to the directly tested refinement.
record.gate_note: The paper cites Toy Models of Superposition and discusses superposition theory, but does not reproduce its toy-network experiments. Results comparing SAE features with neurons and assessing feature coverage or splitting bear directly on V4 or V5. Steering examples deliberately induce behaviors, so they are not treated as evidence that those behaviors arise spontaneously. Cited results from other work are excluded.
record.test_reason: Applies SAE dictionary learning to a production LLM (Claude 3 Sonnet), a new setting. It reports its own results on whether sparse features are recoverable and distinct from neurons (V4). It also reports completeness and feature splitting across dictionary sizes, which qualify V5. T3 fits better than T5: the paper's main aim is to scale the method, and the V5 qualifications are secondary findings.
record.authors_conclusion: Mostly correct. The authors conclude that SAEs scale to Claude 3 Sonnet and yield interpretable, abstract, multilingual/multimodal and causally steerable features. They stress that the feature set is incomplete (likely by orders of magnitude) and that faithfulness cannot be rigorously evaluated. They call superposition a pragmatically useful but not well tested theory, noting multidimensional feature manifolds are plausible.
record.recipe_differences: Applies sparse autoencoders to the middle-layer residual stream of a production-scale finetuned LLM; it does not reproduce the original toy-network training setup or its superposition measurements.
record.method_sensitivity: Feature coverage changes with SAE dictionary size and concept frequency; the analysis uses the middle layer. The authors note that features can split across SAE sizes.
record.problems: The model size is not reported. SAE interpretability is assessed with proxy methods and automated judgments; the authors say there is no gold-standard objective for feature quality and no rigorous method to establish faithful capture of computations. Coverage is incomplete, frequency is measured using a proxy for training data, and the feature-size comparison does not establish stability across methods or runs.
record.rows_left_out: No separate rows for the many individual feature visualizations or deliberately induced steering examples: they do not directly test V4's feature-distribution claim or V5's completeness/stability claim. No toy-model or feature-dimensionality results are reported.

untested.parts: No toy networks, sparsity sweep, phase transition or regular geometry.
No test of whether importance or capacity determines dedicated versus shared dimensions.
No test of non-capacity causes of polysemanticity.
Does not directly measure how many neurons each feature spreads across. Shows only weak maximum correlations with any single neuron.

No comparison across training seeds, SAE architectures, or layers. Features are fit only at the middle-layer residual stream. Faithfulness to model computation is not rigorously established, by the authors' own statement.
No test of 1-D versus multidimensional features. Authors only remark that higher-dimensional feature manifolds 'seem quite plausible'.

missing.what: Larger SAEs contain features for concepts with no analog in the smaller SAE (an earthquake feature group absent from the 1M neighborhood). Bears on stability and completeness.
Reconstruction explains at least 65% of variance. Dead features are about 2%, 35% and 65% for the 1M, 4M and 34M SAEs. Relevant to completeness of the dictionary.
Authors say they are likely 'orders of magnitude short' of all features, even in the middle layer.
Manual inspection of 50 neurons and 50 features: neurons activate in multiple unrelated contexts. Feature activations are also not correlated with any residual-stream basis direction.

record.verdict_notes: This is Scaling Monosemanticity (Templeton et al. 2024), not an original source for the claim. Steering results deliberately induce behaviours and are excluded. Interpretability comparisons rely on Claude-based judges and report no effect sizes. The model size is undisclosed.

versions.untested_parts: No small toy networks, feature-sparsity sweep, transition, or regular-geometry test.
Does not test whether feature importance determines dedicated versus shared neuron dimensions or whether capacity pressure causes polysemanticity.
Neuron polysemanticity is compared with SAE feature interpretability, but the study does not test whether polysemanticity arises for reasons other than capacity pressure.
Tests SAE-extracted features in Claude 3 Sonnet and compares them with neurons; does not test whether features are broadly distributed across multiple neurons as a distinct alternative.
Tests feature coverage and reports feature splitting across SAE sizes. Does not establish whether the units are stable or canonical across methods, training runs, or model changes.
Does not compare one-dimensional feature directions against multidimensional feature representations.

rows.subject: Claude 3 Sonnet
rows.operation_detail: Measured the strongest correlation between sampled 1M SAE feature activations and neurons in preceding layers.

conditions.value: random subset of features; size not stated

rows.value: For 82% of features, the most-correlated neuron has a correlation of 0.3 or smaller.
rows.note: Authors also report that the best-matching neurons showed almost no resemblance in semantic content on manual inspection of a random set of features.
rows.check: Subject is features of the 1M SAE (random subset, size not stated). There is no baseline or chance correlation. Fine otherwise.

source_check.locator_found: Section 2.3, p. 19: Pearson correlations for randomly sampled 1M SAE features against every neuron in all preceding layers.

rows.subject: Claude 3 Sonnet
rows.operation_detail: Compared automated interpretability of randomly selected SAE features and MLP neurons.

conditions.value: 100 randomly chosen features and 100 randomly chosen neurons

rows.measure: Automated interpretability, using explanations and predictions of held-out activations
rows.value: Randomly selected SAE features were significantly more interpretable on average.
rows.note: The text does not give a numeric effect size.
rows.check: No effect size or test is reported in the text. The judge is Claude 3 Opus, so the result depends on the automated-interpretability pipeline.

source_check.locator_found: Section 2.3, p. 20: 100 randomly chosen features versus 100 randomly chosen neurons; Claude 3 Opus explanations and held-out activation predictions.

rows.subject: Claude 3 Sonnet
rows.operation_detail: Compared specificity of random SAE features with neurons using the automated rubric.

conditions.value: random selection of SAE features; compared with neurons in the previous layer

rows.value: Randomly selected SAE features were significantly more specific.
rows.note: The text does not give a numeric effect size.
rows.check: No effect size is reported. The specificity rubric is scored by Claude 3 Opus.

source_check.locator_found: Section 2.3, p. 21; specificity rubric and Claude 3 Opus scoring described in Section 2.1.1, pp. 8–9.

rows.subject: Claude 3 Sonnet
rows.operation_detail: Searched for SAE features corresponding to concepts and had a human rater assess the top five feature explanations for each concept.
rows.measure: Share of London boroughs for which a corresponding feature could be found
rows.note: The authors state that this is evidence that the extracted feature set is incomplete, despite Claude 3 Sonnet being able to list all the boroughs when asked.
rows.check: Completeness is about 60% for London boroughs in the 34M SAE. That is clearly incomplete relative to 'complete units'. The concept set is a single illustrative family.

rows.subject: Claude 3 Sonnet
rows.operation_detail: Compared concept-specific features across SAE dictionary sizes.
rows.measure: Number of finer-grained features corresponding to a feature in the smaller SAE
rows.value: 4M SAE: two features; 34M SAE: eleven fine-grained features
rows.note: The authors describe this as feature splitting as dictionary size increases; the result qualifies the idea that features are stable, canonical units.
rows.check: For V5's claim of stable, canonical units, splitting means the unit set changes with dictionary size: no stability. State should be absent rather than partial. The locator is Section 3.1.1 (correct).

rows.subject: Claude 3 Sonnet
rows.operation_detail: Related concept frequency in a proxy for SAE training data to whether a corresponding feature was found.

conditions.value: elements, cities, animals, and foods (fruits and vegetables)

rows.measure: Feature coverage as a function of concept frequency
rows.value: Larger SAEs tended to have features for rarer concepts; after rescaling by the number of alive features, category curves approximately overlapped and followed a sigmoid-like curve in log-frequency space.
rows.note: Authors caution that frequency was measured in a proxy for training data and that absence of a dedicated feature does not mean the concept is absent from reconstructed activations.
rows.check: Coverage depends on concept frequency and on the number of alive features. The 34M SAE has only about 12M alive features. Frequency is measured in a proxy of the training data.

relationships.condition: 1M SAE features versus MLP neurons and residual basis directions, Claude 3 Sonnet middle layer
relationships.reason: For 82% of sampled features the best neuron correlation is ≤0.3 (r1). Random SAE features were judged more interpretable (r2) and more specific (r3) than neurons. The comparisons use Claude 3 Opus as judge and give no effect sizes.
relationships.display_finding: For 82% of sampled features the best neuron correlation was at most 0.3, and random features were judged more interpretable and more specific than neurons. Claude 3 Opus served as judge, and no effect sizes are given.

source_check.label: supports
source_check.condition: 1M SAE features versus MLP neurons and residual basis directions, Claude 3 Sonnet middle layer
source_check.reason: Section 2.3 reports recoverable sparse features distinct from individual neurons and residual coordinates, with higher automated interpretability and specificity than neurons (r1–r3).

relationships.condition: 34M SAE concept coverage, and San Francisco feature identity across the 1M/4M/34M SAEs
relationships.reason: Features were found for only about 60% of London boroughs, though the model can list them all (r4). One 1M feature splits into 2 and then 11 features as the dictionary grows, so the units are not stable across scale (r5).
relationships.display_finding: Features were found for only about 60% of London boroughs although the model can list them all, and one 1M feature split into 2 and then 11 features as the dictionary grew.

source_check.label: challenges
source_check.condition: 34M SAE concept coverage, and San Francisco feature identity across the 1M/4M/34M SAEs
source_check.reason: Sections 3.1.1 and 3.2 report one San Francisco feature splitting into two and eleven, and only about 60% borough coverage despite demonstrated model knowledge; stable, complete dictionary units fail in these comparisons.

relationships.condition: Coverage of elements, cities, animals and foods across dictionary sizes
relationships.reason: Whether a concept gets a feature depends on its training-data frequency relative to the number of alive features (r6). Completeness is therefore a function of dictionary scale.
relationships.display_finding: Coverage of elements, cities, animals and foods depended on each concept's training-data frequency relative to the number of alive features, so completeness was a function of dictionary scale.

source_check.reason: Section 3.2 finds concept-feature coverage depends on frequency and dictionary scale, with frequency curves approximately aligning after scaling by alive-feature count.

tranche.reason: Tests sparse-feature recovery in a production-scale finetuned LLM, extending the setting beyond toy networks; also reports dictionary incompleteness and splitting.

source_check.notes: The report is dated May 21, 2024; the arXiv header is May 28, 2026. Missing dedicated concept features do not establish missing information: the authors explicitly allow compositional encoding.
